explanations.answer: Has him beaten and put in the stocks
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Pashhur hears Jeremiah prophesying and has Jeremiah the prophet beaten and put in the stocks at the Upper Gate of Benjamin (Jeremiah 20:2). Pashhur is the chief official in the house of the LORD, so he's the one who should know better. I think this is a hard one to read, friend.

explanations.answer: Asks him to pray for the whole city
explanations.explanation: I wish it went that way, friend, but the text doesn't say that. It says Pashhur had Jeremiah beaten and put in the stocks (Jeremiah 20:2). Nothing in the verse mentions a request for prayer. A chief official who hears a warning and reaches for the stocks is a hard scene to picture, I think.

explanations.answer: Brings him before the elders to explain
explanations.explanation: A meeting with the elders sounds so civilized, doesn't it? But the text says Pashhur had Jeremiah beaten and put in the stocks at the Upper Gate of Benjamin (Jeremiah 20:2). The elders don't come up in these verses. I think that tells us how he took the message.

explanations.answer: Gives him a new name from the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! When Pashhur releases Jeremiah from the stocks, Jeremiah says to him, "The LORD does not call you Pashhur, but Magor-missabib." (Jeremiah 20:3). That's a new name straight from the LORD. Jeremiah just spent a night in the stocks, and he still has the LORD's word to deliver.

explanations.answer: Thanks him for letting him go free
explanations.explanation: Thank-you note? Nope, friend. The text doesn't record Jeremiah thanking Pashhur. He tells him, "The LORD does not call you Pashhur, but Magor-missabib." (Jeremiah 20:3). I think that's a very different kind of goodbye.

explanations.answer: Promises to stop prophesying there
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but being in the stocks didn't stop Jeremiah from speaking. He speaks right to Pashhur and says, "The LORD does not call you Pashhur, but Magor-missabib." (Jeremiah 20:3). The text records no promise to stop. He keeps going.

explanations.answer: terror
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says, "I will make you a terror to yourself and to all your friends." (Jeremiah 20:4). That's what the name Magor-missabib is pointing to. It's a heavy word, so I'll say it plain: it's a hard thing to hear.

explanations.answer: blessing
explanations.explanation: Wish it were a blessing, friend, but no. The LORD says, "I will make you a terror to yourself and to all your friends." (Jeremiah 20:4). A name like Magor-missabib doesn't sound like a blessing, and it isn't one. This word is a hard one.

explanations.answer: warning
explanations.explanation: Close in spirit, baker, but that's not the word. The LORD says, "I will make you a terror to yourself and to all your friends." (Jeremiah 20:4). A warning is something you hear, but the LORD says Pashhur himself will be a terror, to himself and to his friends. It's heavy, so take it slow.

explanations.answer: Babylon
explanations.explanation: Babylon is right, baker. The LORD says, "…I will hand Judah over to the king of Babylon…" (Jeremiah 20:4). That reaches past one man in the stocks, since it's all of Judah being handed over. The message was never just about Pashhur.

explanations.answer: Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt is a good guess, friend, but the LORD names a different king. He says He will hand Judah over to the king of Babylon, and that king will carry them away to Babylon (Jeremiah 20:4). Babylon is the word that goes in the blank.

explanations.answer: Assyria
explanations.explanation: Assyria is a good guess, friend, but it's not the word here. The LORD says, "…I will hand Judah over to the king of Babylon…" (Jeremiah 20:4). Babylon is the word that goes in the blank.

explanations.answer: Enemies will carry it all off
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The LORD says He will give the wealth of this city to their enemies, and they will plunder it, seize it and carry it off to Babylon (Jeremiah 20:5). That includes all the treasures of the kings of Judah. Nothing on that list gets left behind.

explanations.answer: It will be buried under the temple
explanations.explanation: Hiding the treasure is a clever plan, friend, but it's not the one the LORD gives. He says He will give the wealth of the city to their enemies, who will plunder it, seize it and carry it off to Babylon (Jeremiah 20:5). Burying it under the temple isn't in these verses. What the LORD describes is the treasure being carried off.

explanations.answer: It will go to the poor of Judah
explanations.explanation: That would be a very different ending, baker. But the LORD says He will give the city's wealth to their enemies. They will plunder it, seize it and carry it off to Babylon (Jeremiah 20:5). The poor of Judah aren't mentioned in these verses.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: True, baker. The LORD says, "And you, Pashhur, and all who live in your house, will go into captivity." (Jeremiah 20:6). Notice that it's his whole house, not just him. The word lands right on his own front door.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: It's true, friend. The LORD says, "And you, Pashhur, and all who live in your house, will go into captivity." (Jeremiah 20:6). That includes everyone in his house, not just him. I think the word hits hard when it comes this close to home.

explanations.answer: He will die and be buried there
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The LORD says, "You will go to Babylon, and there you will die and be buried…" (Jeremiah 20:6). It's a sober ending, and the text doesn't soften it. Pashhur goes to Babylon, and there he dies and is buried.

explanations.answer: He will rise to serve the king
explanations.explanation: Working for the king of Babylon sounds like a promotion, friend, but that's not in the text. The LORD says, "You will go to Babylon, and there you will die and be buried…" (Jeremiah 20:6). Nothing here says Pashhur serves anybody there. This ending is a heavy one.

explanations.answer: He will escape and come home
explanations.explanation: I'd love a happy homecoming, friend, but that's not what the LORD says. He says, "You will go to Babylon, and there you will die and be buried…" (Jeremiah 20:6). His words end with Pashhur dying and being buried in Babylon, and they mention no escape or trip home. It's a sad line.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. The LORD says Pashhur has been prophesying lies to his friends: "…you and all your friends to whom you have prophesied these lies." (Jeremiah 20:6). So the text calls what he said lies, not truth. Jeremiah's message is the one that came from the LORD.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: False is right, baker. The LORD says Pashhur's friends are the ones "…to whom you have prophesied these lies." (Jeremiah 20:6). So what Pashhur prophesied to them was lies, not the truth. I think that makes the stocks sit even heavier.
